identity.title: Large Language Models Develop Novel Social Biases Through Adaptive Exploration

problem.claim: Assess and mitigate social bias in LLMs used for consequential decisions.

gap.claim: Removing pre-existing model biases may not address biases that models develop through experience.

contributions.claim: Demonstrates that LLMs can spontaneously develop biases toward artificial demographic groups despite no inherent group differences.
Relates emergent bias to insufficient exploration in the exploration–exploitation trade-off.
Examines interventions targeting inputs, problem structure, and explicit steering, reporting explicit exploration incentives as the most robust reducer of stratification.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish newly developed, experience-based LLM social biases from merely reflected human biases.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report highly stratified task allocations associated with the novel biases, with lower fairness than assignments by human participants.
The authors report that stratification is exacerbated in newer and larger models.
The authors report that explicitly incentivizing exploration most robustly reduces stratification among the examined interventions.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLMs making real decisions create a need to ensure unbiased behavior.
The paper argues that removing existing biases is insufficient because models may generate new social biases.
Novel group biases produce stratified allocations; the authors connect this pattern to insufficient exploration and early observations shaping group impressions.
Across interventions spanning inputs, structure, and steering, exploration incentives are reported as the strongest mitigation, motivating multifaceted objectives.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates pre-existing bias removal from experience-based bias formation and tests exploration incentives as a mitigation target.

lessons.interpretation: A useful paper frame can connect a newly identified failure mode to a specific behavioral mechanism and intervention dimension.
lessons.application: When presenting an emergent failure mode, define its distinction from the standard failure, propose a mechanism, and align interventions with that mechanism.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the mechanism is only speculative or when the proposed intervention is not actually examined.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the task, participant or model counts, fairness metrics, intervention details, or statistical uncertainty.
It does not establish why newer and larger models show greater stratification or whether exploration incentives generalize beyond the studied paradigm.
